claims.claim: The cephalic male (CEM) and shared inner labial (IL2) neurons are the only known ciliated EV-releasing neurons (EVNs) as defined by imaging of fluorescently-tagged EV cargos released outside the animal.
claims.source: The cephalic male (CEM) and shared inner labial (IL2) neurons are the only known ciliated EV-releasing neurons (EVNs) as defined by imaging of fluorescently-tagged EV cargos released outside the animal (Wang et al., 2014a).
claims.evidence: This is a statement based on previous work from the authors' lab supported by citation.

claims.claim: In C. elegans, EVs are 'shed' at the ciliary base and retained within lumens of the cephalic and inner labial sensory organs as visualized by transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and tomography reconstructions.
claims.source: In C. elegans, EVs are 'shed' at the ciliary base and retained within lumens of the cephalic and inner labial sensory organs as visualized by transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and tomography reconstructions.
claims.evidence: This is based on previous TEM observations from the authors' work.

claims.claim: EVs are also 'released' from cilia directly into the environment outside of the sensory organs, as observed by fluorescently-tagged EV cargos such as the TRP polycystin PKD-2::GFP and myristoylated peripheral membrane protein CIL-7.
claims.source: EVs are also 'released' from cilia directly into the environment outside of the sensory organs, as observed by fluorescently-tagged EV cargos such as the TRP polycystin PKD-2::GFP and myristoylated peripheral membrane protein CIL-7 (Wang et al., 2014a; Maguire et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is based on previous fluorescence microscopy observations supported by citations.

claims.claim: In C. elegans amphid and phasmid cilia, RAB-28 is a BBS-8-dependent IFT cargo that associates with the periciliary membrane (PCM) when in a GTP-bound conformation.
claims.source: In C. elegans amphid and phasmid cilia, RAB-28 is a BBS-8-dependent IFT cargo that associates with the periciliary membrane (PCM) when in a GTP-bound conformation (Jensen et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is based on previous work from the authors' lab supported by citation.

claims.claim: C. elegans RAB-28 disruption leads to defects in amphid sensory compartment size via a proposed cell non-autonomous mechanism, previously speculated to involve EVs.
claims.source: Functionally, C. elegans RAB-28 disruption leads to defects in amphid sensory compartment size via a proposed cell non-autonomous mechanism, previously speculated to involve EVs (Jensen et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is based on previous work from the authors' lab supported by citation.

claims.claim: RAB-28 is significantly overrepresented in a C. elegans EVN transcriptome.
claims.source: An EV-related function for RAB-28 is also suggested by its significant overrepresentation in a C. elegans EVN transcriptome (Wang et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is based on transcriptome data from previous work supported by citation.

claims.claim: GFP-RAB-28Q95L mislocalization in the amphid and phasmid cilia of bbs-5(gk507) worms is indistinguishable from bbs-8(nx77) mutants; GFP signals are diffused throughout the neurons, with no detectable PCM enrichment or IFT movement.
claims.source: We found that GFP-RAB-28Q95L mislocalization in the amphid and phasmid cilia of bbs-5(gk507) worms is indistinguishable from bbs-8(nx77) mutants; GFP signals are diffused throughout the neurons, with no detectable PCM enrichment or IFT movement (Figure 1, enhanced contrast images and expressivity shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and C).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1.

claims.claim: arl-6(ok3472) mutants display a weaker phenotype, with modestly reduced levels of RAB-28 at the PCM and a diffuse dendritic localization.
claims.source: By contrast, arl-6(ok3472) mutants display a weaker phenotype, with modestly reduced levels of RAB-28 at the PCM and a diffuse dendritic localization (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1.

claims.claim: In arl-6 phasmid cilia, the frequency of GFP-RAB-28Q95L- positive IFT trains is increased twofold.
claims.source: Also, in arl-6 phasmid cilia, the frequency of GFP-RAB-28Q95L- positive IFT trains is increased twofold (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and Video 1).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by quantitative microscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: A complete and properly regulated BBSome is required for normal targeting and retention of RAB-28 to the PCM.
claims.source: These data indicate that a complete and properly regulated BBSome is required for normal targeting and retention of RAB-28 to the PCM and that ARL-6 inhibits RAB-28 association with IFT trains, at least in amphid and phasmid neurons.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on RAB-28 localization in BBSome mutants.

claims.claim: ARL-6 inhibits RAB-28 association with IFT trains, at least in amphid and phasmid neurons.
claims.source: These data indicate that a complete and properly regulated BBSome is required for normal targeting and retention of RAB-28 to the PCM and that ARL-6 inhibits RAB-28 association with IFT trains, at least in amphid and phasmid neurons.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing increased IFT frequency in arl-6 mutants.

claims.claim: The PCM localization of GFP-RAB-28Q95L remains intact in pdl-1(gk157) and arl-3(1703) null mutants, but the reporter's IFT motility is completely lost.
claims.source: We found that whilst the PCM localization of GFP-RAB-28Q95L remains intact, the reporter's IFT motility is completely lost in pdl-1(gk157) and arl-3(1703) null mutants (Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1.

claims.claim: PDL-1 is required for RAB-28 association with IFT trains in amphid and phasmid neurons, although it is dispensable for RAB-28 targeting to the PCM of these cells.
claims.source: Thus, like the BBSome, the lipidated protein shuttle PDL-1 is also required for RAB-28 association with IFT trains in amphid and phasmid neurons, although it is dispensable for RAB-28 targeting to the PCM of these cells.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on RAB-28 localization in pdl-1 mutants.

claims.claim: In pdl-1(gk157);arl-6(ok3472) worms, the reduced GFP::RAB-28Q95L PCM localization phenocopies that of the arl-6(ok3472) single mutant.
claims.source: Similarly, in pdl-1(gk157);arl-6(ok3472) worms, the reduced GFP::RAB-28Q95L PCM localization phenocopies that of the arl-6(ok3472) single mutant, although there are additional diffuse signals in the cilium and distal dendrite (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from double mutant analysis supported by microscopy data.

claims.claim: pdl-1 loss strongly suppresses the increased IFT frequency phenotype associated with arl-6 disruption.
claims.source: With regard to RAB-28's IFT behavior phenotype, pdl-1 loss strongly suppresses the increased IFT frequency phenotype associated with arl-6 disruption, further supporting the critical role of PDL-1 in regulating RAB-28 loading onto IFT trains (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C and Video 1).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from double mutant analysis supported by quantitative microscopy data.

claims.claim: arl-6 and pdl-1 mutations are mutually suppressive, consistent with an opposing relationship in regulating the formation of RAB-28-positive IFT trains.
claims.source: Since detectable IFT was never observed in the pdl-1(gk157) single mutant, the latter suggests that arl-6 and pdl-1 mutations are mutually suppressive, consistent with an opposing relationship in regulating the formation of RAB-28-positive IFT trains.
claims.evidence: This is a genetic interpretation based on the double mutant analysis data.

claims.claim: Activated RAB-28 is initially targeted to the PCM by the BBSome, and to a lesser extent ARL-6, and subsequently solubilized by PDL-1 for loading onto IFT trains, a step inhibited by ARL-6 in amphid and phasmid neurons.
claims.source: Taken together, these data reveal a ciliary trafficking pathway in amphid and phasmid neurons whereby activated RAB-28 is initially targeted to the PCM by the BBSome, and to a lesser extent ARL-6, and subsequently solubilized by PDL-1 for loading onto IFT trains, a step inhibited by ARL-6 (summarized in Figure 1 schematic).
claims.evidence: This is a model synthesized from the experimental data on RAB-28 localization in various mutants.

claims.claim: There are 27 classified EVNs in C. elegans that include six IL2 head neurons of males and hermaphrodites and twenty one male-specific neurons (four CEM head neurons; 16 RnB tail ray neurons; one HOB tail hook neuron).
claims.source: There are 27 classified EVNs in C. elegans that include six IL2 head neurons of males and hermaphrodites and twenty one male-specific neurons (four CEM head neurons; 16 RnB tail ray neurons; one HOB tail hook neuron) (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is a statement about C. elegans anatomy based on previous work and confirmed by expression data in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: rab-28 is expressed in the IL2 neurons present in both males and hermaphrodites, as well as all 21 male-specific EVNs.
claims.source: rab-28 is expressed in the IL2 neurons present in both males and hermaphrodites, as well as all 21 male-specific EVNs (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by expression data shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: RAB-28 is enriched at the PCM of CEM and RnB neurons.
claims.source: Like amphid and phasmid channel neurons, RAB-28 is enriched at the PCM of CEM and RnB neurons (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: Unlike amphid and phasmid cells, a pool of RAB-28 also occurs within the distal ends of the CEM and ray RnB cilia.
claims.source: However, unlike amphid and phasmid cells, a pool of RAB-28 also occurs within the distal ends of the CEM and ray RnB cilia (see arrowheads in Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: Moving RAB-28-positive IFT particles were rarely detected in CEM and RnB cilia.
claims.source: Moving RAB-28-positive IFT particles were rarely detected in CEM and RnB cilia (Figure 2C and Video 2), consistent with our previous report showing that IFT in CEM cilia is less frequent than in amphid cilia (Morsci and Barr, 2011).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2C and Video 2.

claims.claim: Almost all detectable RAB-28-positive IFT trains in male EVN cilia move in the retrograde direction.
claims.source: Interestingly, almost all detectable RAB-28-positive IFT trains in male EVN cilia move in the retrograde direction (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: RAB-28 is not an EV cargo.
claims.source: We did not observe RAB-28 in environmentally-released EVs, indicating that RAB-28 is not an EV cargo.
claims.evidence: This is a negative finding from microscopy observations.

claims.claim: GFP::RAB-28Q95L PCM localization was absent in bbs-5(gk507) and bbs-8(nx77) males in EVN cilia.
claims.source: In EVN cilia, GFP::RAB-28Q95L PCM localization was absent in bbs-5(gk507) and bbs-8(nx77) males, whilst reduced in arl-6(ok3472) and pdl-1(gk157) males (Figure 2B), similar to phenotypes observed in the amphid and phasmid channel neuronal cilia (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: GFP::RAB-28Q95L PCM localization was reduced in arl-6(ok3472) and pdl-1(gk157) males in EVN cilia.
claims.source: In EVN cilia, GFP::RAB-28Q95L PCM localization was absent in bbs-5(gk507) and bbs-8(nx77) males, whilst reduced in arl-6(ok3472) and pdl-1(gk157) males (Figure 2B), similar to phenotypes observed in the amphid and phasmid channel neuronal cilia (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: The distal pool of RAB-28 in CEM and RnB cilia was reduced or absent in bbs-5, bbs-8, arl-6, and pdl-1 mutants.
claims.source: Also, the distal pool of RAB-28 in CEM and RnB cilia was reduced or absent in all of these mutants (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: IFT movement of RAB-28Q95L was absent in bbs-5(gk507), bbs-8(nx77) and pdl-1(gk157) mutant EVN cilia.
claims.source: Like in amphid and phasmid neurons, IFT movement of RAB-28Q95L was also absent in bbs-5(gk507), bbs-8(nx77) and pdl-1(gk157) mutant EVN cilia.
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from microscopy observations.

claims.claim: RAB-28Q95L IFT movement was not detectable in the EVN cilia of arl-6(ok3472) males, which is in striking contrast to the increased frequency of RAB-28-positive IFT trains in amphid and phasmid neurons.
claims.source: Surprisingly, RAB-28Q95L IFT movement was also not detectable in the EVN cilia of arl-6(ok3472) males, which is in striking contrast to the increased frequency of RAB-28-positive IFT trains in amphid and phasmid neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding highlighting cell-type specific differences.

claims.claim: In pdl-1(gk157);arl-6(ok3472) double mutant EVNs, GFP::RAB-28Q95L is diffusely localized in the cytoplasm, with no PCM enrichment.
claims.source: Analysis of pdl-1(gk157);arl-6(ok3472) double mutant EVNs revealed that GFP::RAB-28Q95L is diffusely localized in the cytoplasm, with no PCM enrichment (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from double mutant analysis supported by microscopy data.

claims.claim: pdl-1 and arl-6 demonstrate an additive genetic relationship in targeting RAB-28 to EVN cilia, which is in contrast to that of amphid and phasmid neurons where the relationship is suppressive.
claims.source: Thus, pdl-1 and arl-6 demonstrate an additive genetic relationship in targeting RAB-28 to EVN cilia, which is in contrast to that of amphid and phasmid neurons where the relationship is suppressive.
claims.evidence: This is a genetic interpretation based on the double mutant analysis data showing cell-type specific differences.

claims.claim: bbs-5(gk507) and bbs-8(nx77) mutant hermaphrodites abnormally accumulate electron dense matrix filled vesicles in the sheath cell process similar to RAB-28T26N-overexpressing worms.
claims.source: We found that bbs-5(gk507) and bbs-8(nx77) mutant hermaphrodites abnormally accumulate electron dense matrix filled vesicles in the sheath cell process similar to RAB-28T26N-overexpressing worms, although sometimes at higher levels (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by TEM data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: bbs-5(gk507) and bbs-8(nx77) mutant hermaphrodites consistently exhibit highly distended amphid compartments, 2–3 times the size of WT, although with much darker staining of the extracellular matrix (ECM).
claims.source: Additionally, much like hermaphrodites overexpressing RAB-28Q95L (GTP-preferring) (Jensen et al., 2016), bbs-5(gk507) and bbs-8(nx77) mutant hermaphrodites consistently exhibit highly distended amphid compartments,2–3 times the size of WT,although with much darker staining of the extracellular matrix (ECM) (Figure 3A,B).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by TEM data shown in Figure 3A,B.

claims.claim: At the level of the ciliary middle segments and transition zones, where the compartment is most enlarged, bbs-5(gk507) and bbs-8(nx77) mutant compartments each contain 11 ciliary axonemes, instead of the usual 10.
claims.source: Also, at the level of the ciliary middle segments and transition zones, where the compartment is most enlarged, bbs-5(gk507) and bbs-8(nx77) mutant compartments each contain 11 ciliary axonemes, instead of the usual 10 (Figure 3B,C).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by TEM data shown in Figure 3B,C.

claims.claim: In arl-6(ok3472) mutant, whilst there are electron dense deposits in the sheath cell at the ciliary middle segment, transition zone and PCMC levels of the amphid sensory organ, compartment size and ECM density are normal.
claims.source: A weaker phenotype was observed in the arl-6(ok3472) mutant; whilst there are electron dense deposits in the sheath cell at the ciliary middle segment, transition zone and PCMC levels of the amphid sensory organ, compartment size and ECM density are normal (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by TEM data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: Disruption of the BBSome, or ARL-6 to a lesser extent, phenocopies the amphid sensory organ and sheath cell defects observed in rab-28-disrupted worms.
claims.source: Together, these data show that disruption of the BBSome, or ARL-6 to a lesser extent, phenocopies the amphid sensory organ and sheath cell defects observed in rab-28-disrupted worms (overexpressing RAB-28T26N or RAB-28Q95L).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing TEM data across different mutants.

claims.claim: C. elegans BBS genes are expressed exclusively in ciliated neurons.
claims.source: As with rab-28, C. elegans BBS genes are expressed exclusively in ciliated neurons (Ansley et al., 2003; Fan et al., 2004), indicating that their effects on the amphid sheath cell are also likely due to cell non-autonomous functions.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about BBS gene expression supported by citations.

claims.claim: The effects of BBS genes on the amphid sheath cell are likely due to cell non-autonomous functions.
claims.source: As with rab-28, C. elegans BBS genes are expressed exclusively in ciliated neurons (Ansley et al., 2003; Fan et al., 2004), indicating that their effects on the amphid sheath cell are also likely due to cell non-autonomous functions.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the expression pattern of BBS genes and the observed sheath cell phenotypes.

claims.claim: In the amphids, the BBSome, ARL-6 and RAB-28 function together in a common cell non-autonomous pathway that regulates sensory organ size.
claims.source: Thus, in the amphids, the BBSome, ARL-6 and RAB-28 function together in a common cell non-autonomous pathway that regulates sensory organ size.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the phenotypic similarities between rab-28 and BBSome mutants.

claims.claim: In rab-28(tm2636) mutant males, total PKD-2::GFP levels at the CEM ciliary region from the PCMC to the tip are similar to control.
claims.source: In rab-28(tm2636) mutant males, total PKD-2::GFP levels at the CEM ciliary region from the PCMC to the tip are similar to control (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by quantitative microscopy data shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: rab-28(tm2636) mutants display abnormally high PKD-2::GFP levels at more distal parts of the CEM cilium region, indicating a ciliary localization defective (Cil) phenotype.
claims.source: However, fluorescence intensity measurement analyses revealed a subtle yet consistent change in the pattern of PKD-2::GFP distribution in rab-28(tm2636) males indicating a ciliary localization defective (Cil) phenotype. Specifically, unlike control animals where PKD-2::GFP is most intense at the PCMC region of the CEM cilium, rab-28(tm2636) mutants display abnormally high PKD-2::GFP levels at more distal parts of the CEM cilium region (Figure 4B,C).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by quantitative microscopy data shown in Figure 4B,C.

claims.claim: Control and rab-28(tm2636) males release similar numbers of PKD-2::GFP-labeled EVs.
claims.source: We found that control and rab-28(tm2636) males release similar numbers of PKD-2::GFP-labeled EVs, ruling out a function for RAB-28 in environmental EV release of PKD-2 and suggesting a possible defect whereby EV shedding into the sensory organ lumen is abnormally upregulated (Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by quantitative microscopy data shown in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: RAB-28 is not required for the release of PKD-2-positive EVs into the environment.
claims.source: We found that control and rab-28(tm2636) males release similar numbers of PKD-2::GFP-labeled EVs, ruling out a function for RAB-28 in environmental EV release of PKD-2 and suggesting a possible defect whereby EV shedding into the sensory organ lumen is abnormally upregulated (Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the EV release quantification data.

claims.claim: The rab-28(tm2636) cephalic sensory organ abnormally accumulates large amounts of CIL-7::GFP in ciliary regions.
claims.source: In contrast to the relatively subtle PKD-2::GFP Cil phenotype, the rab-28(tm2636) cephalic sensory organ abnormally accumulates large amounts of CIL-7::GFP in ciliary regions (Figure 4F–H).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4F–H.

claims.claim: A similar strong Cil phenotype was also observed in rab-28(gk1040) worms.
claims.source: A similar strong Cil phenotype was also observed in rab-28(gk1040) worms (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Wild-type and rab-28(tm2636) males release similar numbers of CIL-7::GFP-containing EVs in mounting media.
claims.source: Wild-type and rab-28(tm2636) males release similar numbers of CIL-7::GFP-containing EVs in mounting media (Figure 4I and Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by quantitative microscopy data.

claims.claim: RAB-28 regulates the abundance and distribution of ciliary proteins expressed in the EV-releasing CEM neurons.
claims.source: These results indicate a role for RAB-28 in regulating the abundance and distribution of ciliary proteins expressed in the EV-releasing CEM neurons.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the PKD-2 and CIL-7 localization data in rab-28 mutants.

claims.claim: RAB-28 is not required for the release of CIL-7-positive EVs into the environment.
claims.source: Our data also indicate that RAB-28 is not required for the release of PKD-2- and CIL-7-positive EVs into the environment.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the EV release quantification data.

claims.claim: bbs-8(nx77) and, to a lesser extent, arl-6(ok3472) mutants show Cil defects, with the ciliary EV marker CIL-7::GFP accumulating at the PCMC and around the axonemal region of CEM cilia.
claims.source: Similar to rab-28 mutants, we found Cil defects in bbs-8(nx77) and, to a lesser extent, arl-6(ok3472) mutants, with the ciliary EV marker CIL-7::GFP accumulating at the PCMC and around the axonemal region of CEM cilia (Figure 4J–L).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4J–L.

claims.claim: pdl-1(gk157) mutants show no gross CIL-7 localization defects.
claims.source: In contrast, pdl-1(gk157) mutants show no gross CIL-7 localization defects (Figure 4J,L).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4J,L.

claims.claim: bbs-8(nx77), arl-6(ok372) and pdl-1(gk157) mutant males show no defect in the number of CIL-7-labeled EVs released into the media.
claims.source: Similar to rab-28 mutant males, we found no defect in the number of CIL-7-labeled EVs released into the media by bbs-8(nx77), arl-6(ok372) and pdl-1(gk157) mutant males (Figure 4M,N).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by quantitative microscopy data shown in Figure 4M,N.

claims.claim: RAB-28, BBS-8 and ARL-6, but not PDL-1, regulate the localization and levels of EV markers in the ciliated sensory organs.
claims.source: Together, these data indicate that RAB-28, BBS-8 and ARL-6, but not PDL-1, regulate the localization and levels of EV markers in the ciliated sensory organs.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the CIL-7 and PKD-2 localization data across different mutants.

claims.claim: RAB-28, BBS-8 and ARL-6 do not regulate the release of EVs from the sensory organs into the external environment of the worm.
claims.source: However, they do not regulate the release of EVs from the sensory organs into the external environment of the worm.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the EV release quantification data.

claims.claim: In wild-type males, EVs are observed in the extracellular space of the cephalic sensory organ (ie. the lumen).
claims.source: In wild-type males, EVs are observed in the extracellular space of the cephalic sensory organ (ie. the lumen) (Figure 5B,C and Video 3).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by TEM data shown in Figure 5B,C and Video 3.

claims.claim: In wild-type males, EVs in the cephalic lumen are typically of low electron density and found predominantly in the proximal regions of the lumen, although a few occur in distal regions.
claims.source: These EVs are typically of low electron density and found predominantly in the proximal regions of the lumen, although a few occur in distal regions (Figure 5B; Wang et al., 2014a; Silva et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by TEM data shown in Figure 5B and previous work.

claims.claim: In rab-28(tm2636) male worms, the distal part of the cephalic lumen is enlarged and accumulates an excess of EVs.
claims.source: In rab-28(tm2636) male worms, the distal part of the cephalic lumen is enlarged and accumulates an excess of EVs.
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by TEM data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: rab-28 mutant EVs are smaller and more uniform in size, and sometimes more electron dense, possibly indicating a change in composition.
claims.source: When compared with control counterparts, these rab-28 mutant EVs are smaller and more uniform in size, and sometimes more electron dense, possibly indicating a change in composition (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B, Video 3).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by TEM data with speculative interpretation about composition.

claims.claim: In proximal parts of the lumen, at the level of the CEP and CEM ciliary transition zones and PCMCs, rab-28(tm2636) mutants show increased incidence of electron dense EVs.
claims.source: In proximal parts of the lumen, at the level of the CEP and CEM ciliary transition zones and PCMCs, we also observed increased incidence of electron dense EVs (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C,E,F and Video 3).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by TEM data.

claims.claim: RAB-28 loss disrupts the number and nature of EVs in the lumens of cephalic sensory organs.
claims.source: Thus, RAB-28 loss disrupts the number and nature of EVs in the lumens of cephalic sensory organs.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the TEM data on EVs in rab-28 mutants.

claims.claim: The cephalic sensory organ and CEM ciliary tip in the rab-28(tm2636) mutant retains normal exposure to the environment.
claims.source: Notably, electron tomographic analysis revealed that the cephalic sensory organ and CEM ciliary tip in the rab-28(tm2636) mutant retains normal exposure to the environment, indicating that pore blockage or a ciliogenesis defect is not the cause of EV accumulation in the distal lumen (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by electron tomography data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: rab-28(tm2636) worms retain the normal CEM ciliary axonemal AB tubule split that is important to EV release.
claims.source: Also, rab-28(tm2636) worms retain the normal CEM ciliary axonemal AB tubule split that is important to EV release (Silva et al., 2017; O'Hagan et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding with reference to previous work on the importance of the AB tubule split.

claims.claim: rab-28(tm2636) mutant males produce and shed excessive amounts of abnormally stained and sized EVs into the cephalic sensory organ.
claims.source: We conclude from these data that rab-28(tm2636) mutant males produce and shed excessive amounts of abnormally stained and sized EVs into the cephalic sensory organ.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the TEM data on EVs in rab-28 mutants.

claims.claim: RAB-28 regulates EV cargo sorting and production (biogenesis).
claims.source: These data suggest that RAB-28 regulates EV cargo sorting and production (biogenesis) and that RAB-28 acts as a negative regulator of EV shedding without affecting environmental EV release.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the TEM and fluorescence microscopy data on EVs in rab-28 mutants.

claims.claim: RAB-28 acts as a negative regulator of EV shedding without affecting environmental EV release.
claims.source: These data suggest that RAB-28 regulates EV cargo sorting and production (biogenesis) and that RAB-28 acts as a negative regulator of EV shedding without affecting environmental EV release.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined TEM and fluorescence microscopy data.

claims.claim: RAB-28 negatively regulates cephalic sensory compartment size.
claims.source: Our findings also show that RAB-28 negatively regulates cephalic sensory compartment size, in agreement with what we previously reported for RAB-28 in the amphid organs (Jensen et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the TEM data showing enlarged cephalic lumen in rab-28 mutants.

results.result: The BBSome, ARL-6, and PDL-1 regulate RAB-28 trafficking to the periciliary membrane (PCM) and ciliary membranes in amphid and phasmid neurons. The BBSome is required for RAB-28 PCM targeting and retention, while PDL-1 and ARL-3 are required for RAB-28 IFT motility but not PCM localization. ARL-6 inhibits RAB-28 association with IFT trains, and pdl-1 and arl-6 mutations show mutual suppression in regulating RAB-28-positive IFT trains.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C42 provide comprehensive microscopy data (Figures 1 and supplements) showing RAB-28 localization phenotypes in single and double mutants of bbs-5, bbs-8, arl-6, pdl-1, and arl-3. The data consistently demonstrate that BBSome components are required for PCM localization, PDL-1 is required for IFT but not PCM targeting, and genetic epistasis experiments support the proposed trafficking pathway. The quantitative IFT frequency measurements and genetic interaction analyses provide strong converging evidence.

results.result: RAB-28 trafficking in EVN cilia differs from amphid/phasmid neurons in a cell-type-specific manner. In EVNs, RAB-28 localizes to both the PCM and distal ciliary regions, IFT is infrequent and predominantly retrograde, and PDL-1 is partially required for PCM localization (unlike in amphid/phasmid neurons). The genetic relationship between pdl-1 and arl-6 is additive in EVNs rather than suppressive as in amphid/phasmid neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C56 and C108-C110 present expression data (Figure 2A) and localization/IFT analysis (Figure 2B-C) demonstrating cell-type-specific differences in RAB-28 trafficking. The data show distinct localization patterns, IFT frequencies, and genetic interactions in EVN versus amphid/phasmid cilia. The observations are internally consistent and supported by quantitative measurements, though the mechanistic basis for these differences remains to be determined.

results.result: BBSome and ARL-6 mutants phenocopy RAB-28 disruption in causing amphid sensory organ defects, including enlarged compartments, altered ECM staining, extra ciliary axonemes, and electron-dense vesicle accumulation in sheath cells. These effects are cell non-autonomous since BBS genes are expressed exclusively in ciliated neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C64 are supported by TEM data (Figure 3) showing consistent phenotypes across bbs-5, bbs-8, and arl-6 mutants that match previously reported rab-28 phenotypes. The quantitative measurements of compartment size and axoneme number, combined with expression data showing neuronal-specific BBS gene expression, support the cell non-autonomous mechanism. The phenotypic similarities establish a functional relationship between RAB-28 and its trafficking machinery.

results.result: RAB-28, BBS-8, and ARL-6 (but not PDL-1) regulate the localization and levels of EV cargo markers (PKD-2::GFP and CIL-7::GFP) in ciliated sensory organs, causing accumulation in ciliary regions when disrupted. However, these genes do not affect the release of EVs into the external environment.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C78 are supported by comprehensive fluorescence microscopy data (Figure 4) showing altered PKD-2 and CIL-7 distribution in rab-28, bbs-8, and arl-6 mutants but not pdl-1 mutants. Quantitative measurements of fluorescence intensity ratios and EV release counts demonstrate the ciliary localization defects while confirming normal environmental EV release. The data distinguish between EV shedding into lumens versus release into the environment, providing strong evidence for the proposed regulatory roles.

results.result: RAB-28 negatively regulates EV shedding at the ciliary base in cephalic sensory organs. rab-28 mutants accumulate excessive EVs in the distal cephalic lumen that are smaller, more uniform, and sometimes more electron-dense than wild-type EVs. RAB-28 loss does not affect ciliary structure or environmental exposure, indicating the defect is in EV biogenesis/shedding rather than release.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C90 and C2 are strongly supported by high-quality TEM data (Figure 5 and supplements) showing EV accumulation in rab-28 mutants with quantitative measurements of EV numbers in different lumen regions. Electron tomography confirms normal ciliary structure and environmental exposure, ruling out alternative explanations. The characterization of EV size and electron density provides additional evidence for altered EV biogenesis. The convergence of TEM and fluorescence data (from previous result) strongly supports the negative regulatory role.

results.result: The BBSome negatively regulates EV shedding in cephalic organs more strongly than RAB-28, causing more numerous and size-variable EV accumulation throughout the lumen, along with matrix-filled vesicles in sheath glia. The BBSome likely regulates multiple EV regulators beyond RAB-28, and the PCM may be the primary site of RAB-28's EV-related function.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C96, C5, C113-C117 are supported by TEM data (Figure 5D) showing more severe EV phenotypes in bbs-8 mutants compared to rab-28 mutants. The comparative analysis of EV number, size distribution, and spatial distribution provides strong evidence for the BBSome having broader regulatory roles. The inference that the BBSome regulates additional EV regulators is reasonable given the phenotypic differences, though direct identification of these regulators would strengthen the conclusion.

results.result: BBS-8 suppresses ectopic EV shedding in amphid sensory organs in a RAB-28-independent manner. bbs-8 mutants show large EV accumulations throughout the amphid lumen, while rab-28 mutants do not.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C99 are supported by TEM data (Figure 6) showing ectopic EVs in bbs-8 but not rab-28 mutant amphids. This demonstrates a RAB-28-independent function of the BBSome in suppressing EV shedding in non-EVN-containing sensory organs. The observation is clear and well-documented, though the mechanism remains to be elucidated.

results.result: RAB-28 and the BBSome regulate sensory organ morphogenesis, with mutants displaying expanded lumens and abnormal matrix-filled vesicle deposits in sheath cells. The authors propose this occurs via EV-mediated signaling between neurons and glia.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C128-C132 are supported by TEM data showing morphological defects in mutants (Figures 3, 5, 6). However, the proposed mechanism linking EV defects to sensory organ morphogenesis (C132) is speculative. While the correlation between EV accumulation and organ expansion is documented, and prior work supports neuron-glia signaling in organ size regulation (C130-C131), direct evidence that EVs mediate this signaling is lacking. Alternative explanations (physical constraints from accumulated EVs, EV-independent signaling defects) are acknowledged but not ruled out.

results.result: EV shedding at the ciliary base and EV release into the environment are genetically separable processes, with the PCM being a major site of EV ciliary base shedding.
results.evaluation: Claims C119-C120 are supported by the combined evidence that rab-28 and bbs-8 mutants show EV accumulation in lumens but normal environmental release (from previous results), while other mutants (KLP-6, CCPP-1, etc., C118) show the opposite phenotype. This genetic separation provides strong evidence for distinct mechanisms. The PCM localization is consistent with RAB-28 localization data, though the claim acknowledges uncertainty about whether all EVs originate from the PCM.

results.result: The PCM is the primary membrane at which RAB-28 functions, with its levels regulated by the BBSome, IFT, and lipidated protein transport machinery in a cell-specific manner. This represents a potentially general mechanism for ciliary targeting of lipidated proteins.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C107 synthesize the trafficking data from earlier results and place them in the context of prior work on Rab28 and INPP5E (C103-C105). The conclusion about PCM being the primary functional site is well-supported by the localization and functional data. The generalization to other lipidated proteins (C106) is appropriately qualified as speculative, and the suggestion that C. elegans RAB-28 could serve as a model system (C107) is reasonable given the findings.

results.result: The accumulated EVs in rab-28 mutant sensory organs arise due to abnormalities in biogenesis and shedding at the ciliary base rather than defects in environmental release.
results.evaluation: Claims C111-C112 are well-supported by the combination of normal environmental EV release (C67, C71) and increased EV accumulation in lumens (C81-C83) demonstrated by both fluorescence microscopy and TEM. The logic is sound and the conclusion is directly supported by the data.

results.result: EVs may mediate signaling between cilia and glia to shape sensory organ compartments, and defects in ciliary EV biogenesis may contribute to human ciliopathies including cone-rod dystrophy and retinitis pigmentosa. The relationship between C. elegans EV shedding and mammalian photoreceptor disc shedding remains unclear.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C9, C134, C137-C138, C140 are appropriately presented as speculative. While the association of RAB28 and BBSome genes with human retinal disease is established (C1, C134), and the C. elegans data demonstrate EV regulatory roles, the connection to human disease pathogenesis is hypothetical. The apparent contradiction between Rab28 positively regulating mouse OS shedding but negatively regulating C. elegans EV shedding (C138) highlights the uncertainty. These are reasonable hypotheses for future investigation but lack direct supporting evidence.

results.result: Ciliary EVs in C. elegans are ectosomes/microvesicles rather than exosomes, based on their size, the absence of multivesicular bodies at the ciliary base, normal EV biogenesis in ESCRT mutants, and observation of omega-shaped vesicle budding.
results.evaluation: Claims C141-C147 are supported by multiple lines of evidence: genetic data showing normal EV biogenesis in ESCRT mutants (C144), TEM observations showing absence of multivesicular bodies (C145), size measurements (C146), and direct observation of omega-shaped budding (C147). The conclusion that these are ectosomes rather than exosomes is well-supported, though the authors appropriately acknowledge the limitations of current EV classification methods.

results.result: A proposed model where defective ciliary protein turnover in Rab28 or BBSome-disrupted worms leads to compensatory EV shedding to remove receptors from ciliary/periciliary membranes.
results.evaluation: Claim C122 is explicitly presented as a speculative model to explain the EV accumulation phenotype. While it draws on prior work linking Rab28 and the BBSome to endosomal sorting (C121) and is consistent with proposed mechanisms in mammalian cells (C123), it lacks direct experimental support in the current study. This is appropriately presented as a hypothesis rather than a conclusion.
